name: No Real-World Advantage Yet
subject: quantum-computing
subjectTitle: A Skeptic's Guide to Quantum Computing

lesson.title: Impressive Demos, Empty Wallets
lesson.summary: Despite headline-grabbing experiments, no quantum computer has yet solved a commercially useful problem faster than the best available classical method; the demonstrated advantages so far are confined to contrived tasks built specifically to favor quantum hardware.
lesson.body:
Quantum advantage, as opposed to the looser and more theatrical term quantum supremacy, is the narrower and more concrete claim that a quantum computer solves some specific problem faster, cheaper, or more accurately than any known classical approach. The bar sounds simple, but meeting it in a way that matters commercially has not happened yet, despite roughly four decades of experimental progress and tens of billions of dollars in public and private investment across governments, universities, and startups.

Every experimental claim of quantum advantage to date rests on a contrived benchmark: a task engineered specifically because it is hard for classical computers to simulate and comparatively natural for a quantum processor to execute, with no requirement that the task be useful to anyone. Random circuit sampling, the basis of Google's 2019 Sycamore claim, is the clearest example. The output is a statistical distribution of essentially random measurement outcomes from a quantum circuit chosen because it resists classical simulation, not because anyone wants that distribution for engineering, finance, medicine, or logistics.

This distinction separates two very different questions that frequently get conflated in press coverage: can a quantum computer do something no classical computer can do in reasonable time, versus can a quantum computer do something useful that a classical computer cannot do as well. The first has been argued, with real controversy, on a handful of occasions. The second has not been convincingly demonstrated for a problem of genuine industrial or scientific value, whether in drug discovery, materials design, cryptography, logistics, or finance, despite persistent claims to the contrary in press releases from quantum computing companies and their investors.

The gap is not for lack of trying. IBM, Google, chemistry and materials science research groups, and numerous startups have run quantum algorithms on real hardware against problems chosen specifically for their practical relevance, including small molecule simulation and portfolio optimization. In essentially every published case so far, either the problem instance tested was too small to be practically interesting on its own, or a classical computer using a well chosen heuristic or approximation method matched or beat the quantum result. This is not a failure of ambition. It reflects the current immaturity of quantum hardware, still limited by noise and short coherence times, combined with a genuinely open scientific question about which real-world problems, if any, are structured the way algorithms like Shor's or Grover's need them to be structured.

None of this means a useful quantum advantage is impossible in principle. It means that, as of today, the honest claim is not yet demonstrated rather than already delivered. A skeptic's job throughout this guide is to hold that distinction clearly rather than let a genuinely difficult, still-open scientific question get rounded up into inevitability by marketing copy or optimistic headlines.
